content: The Surveillance Guide for Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in the WHO South-East Asia Region: Module 3 Poliomyelitis was published in September 2023 by the World Health Organization (WHO). This guide provides detailed instructions and protocols for the surveillance of poliomyelitis in the South-East Asia region, emphasizing the importance of high-quality surveillance to detect poliovirus transmission and support global eradication efforts. The WHO South-East Asia Region was declared free of all wild polioviruses (types 1, 2, and 3) in 2014. Globally, as of 2022, only wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) remains endemic in Afghanistan and Pakistan, while types 2 and 3 have been certified as eradicated in 2015 and 2019, respectively. However, the risk of WPV1 importation into the region persists, along with the potential for outbreaks caused by circulating vaccine-derived polioviruses (cVDPVs). Effective surveillance is critical for timely detection of poliovirus transmission, including WPV, VDPVs, and Sabin-like viruses. Objectives of Polio Surveillance The primary objectives of the polio surveillance system are to: 1. Detect the importation of wild poliovirus (WPV). 2. Identify the presence of vaccine-derived polioviruses (VDPVs) within a country. Types of Polio Surveillance Poliovirus surveillance consists of three main components: 1. Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) Surveillance: This is the cornerstone of polio eradication efforts and is considered the gold standard for detecting poliovirus circulation. 2. Environmental Surveillance (ES): This involves testing sewage or other environmental samples for poliovirus. 3. Surveillance Among Patients with Primary Immunodeficiency Disorders (PID): This focuses on individuals with conditions that may lead to prolonged poliovirus excretion. These surveillance activities are supported by the Global Poliovirus Laboratory Network (GPLN) and the comprehensive Polio Information System, which provide access to data for informed decision-making. Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) Surveillance AFP surveillance is essential for identifying poliovirus circulation. All countries should be capable of detecting suspected AFP cases through at least one of the following strategies: Active Surveillance: Proactive case detection by health workers. Passive Surveillance: Reporting of cases by healthcare providers. Community-Based Surveillance: Involvement of community members in identifying and reporting cases. Linkages to Other Surveillance Systems AFP surveillance should ideally be integrated with case-based surveillance for other vaccine-preventable diseases, such as measles and rubella, as well as with surveillance for immunodeficiency-related VDPVs, enteroviruses, and environmental sampling. Case Detection and Investigation A suspected AFP case is defined as any child under 15 years of age presenting with sudden onset of flaccid paralysis or muscle weakness, or any person of any age with paralytic illness suspected to be poliomyelitis by a physician. The date of onset of paralysis is critical for determining the timeline of investigation and sample collection. All suspected cases must be investigated within 48 hours of notification by trained health staff. Since polio can be clinically indistinguishable from other causes of AFP (e.g., Guillain-Barré syndrome, transverse myelitis), stool specimens must be collected and tested for poliovirus, even if the clinical diagnosis suggests a non-polio cause. Specimen Collection and Transportation Stool specimens are the primary samples for laboratory confirmation of poliovirus. Two stool specimens, collected at least 24 hours apart and within 14 days of paralysis onset, are required. These specimens must be stored and transported under cold chain conditions (4–8°C) to prevent virus degradation. If delays occur, specimens should be frozen and shipped with dry ice or cold packs. Proper labeling and documentation, including the unique epidemiological identification (EPID) number, are essential. Contact Sampling Contact sampling involves collecting stool specimens from three individuals who have been in close contact with an AFP case. This method helps identify asymptomatic poliovirus carriers and provides additional evidence of poliovirus circulation. Contact sampling is particularly important in cases with inadequate stool specimens or in high-risk areas. Laboratory Testing All AFP case specimens must be processed in WHO-accredited laboratories within the GPLN. These laboratories perform: 1. Virus Isolation: Identifying poliovirus in stool samples. 2. Intratypic Differentiation: Determining whether the virus is WPV, VDPV, or Sabin-like using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). 3. Genomic Sequencing: Analyzing the genetic sequence of the virus to track transmission pathways. 60-Day Follow-Up Examination Certain AFP cases require a follow-up examination between 60 and 90 days after paralysis onset to assess for residual paralysis. This follow-up provides additional evidence for classifying the case as polio-compatible or discarded. Case Classification AFP cases are classified as: Confirmed: WPV or VDPV is isolated from stool specimens or those of close contacts. Compatible: Cases without adequate specimens but with clinical and epidemiological features consistent with poliomyelitis. Discarded: Cases with adequate investigation and no evidence of WPV or VDPV infection. Data Management and Analysis A robust information system is critical for effective polio surveillance. Surveillance data should be reviewed weekly at national, state, and district levels to monitor disease trends, assess risks, and evaluate the performance of the AFP surveillance system. Key indicators include the timeliness of case detection, specimen collection, and laboratory reporting. Environmental Surveillance Environmental surveillance involves testing sewage or wastewater for poliovirus. This method complements AFP surveillance and helps detect silent poliovirus circulation in communities. Public Health Response In the event of WPV or VDPV detection, immediate public health interventions, including vaccination campaigns, are necessary to prevent further transmission. This guide underscores the importance of maintaining high-quality surveillance systems to achieve and sustain global polio eradication.
